title: Ekiden Becoming More Popular in UK
paragraphs: Ekiden, a type of long-distance relay race that is hugely popular in Japan, is attracting growing interest in the UK.

In an ekiden race, a team of runners each completes one section of a long course. Instead of passing a baton, as in a track relay, the runners pass a cloth sash called a "tasuki" to the next runner on their team. The format, which is inspired by a centuries-old Japanese tradition, emphasizes teamwork rather than individual performance.

The UK's main ekiden event is the FT Nikkei UK Ekiden, which is supported by the Financial Times newspaper and its Japanese owner, Nikkei. On June 12, 2026, the race was held for the third time. The course stretched about 112 kilometers along the River Thames, from Windsor to Reading.

The event has grown quickly. This year, 17 of the UK's top university athletics teams took part, along with Ritsumeikan University from Japan. In total, there were 35 mixed teams, each made up of ten runners. For the first time, university teams had to qualify to enter, and there is now a waiting list for teams. The race also introduced a new division for teams from companies and communities. Oxford University won the university division by a narrow margin.

The race's popularity reflects wider interest in ekiden in the UK. In 2025, the word "ekiden" was even added to the Oxford English Dictionary. In addition, a "Mini Ekiden" program is being introduced in 50 primary schools across the UK to encourage children to take part.

This year's event also had a special connection to Japan's Ishikawa Prefecture, which was hit by a major earthquake in 2024. Runners from the region took part, and the race medals featured a poem written by a local community.

Anna Dingley, the founder and CEO of the FT Nikkei UK Ekiden, described it as a truly special race that people can aspire to be part of. Matt Seddon, the event's athletics director, added that success depends on the strength of the team rather than the individual, and that there is "nowhere to hide."
